headline: Appledore's Backside Gives Up Haddock, Stripers Chew Through the Hampton Flood
subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline is plenty when you know which fifty yards of ledge to sit on — this week it was the Shoals for groundfish and Hampton Harbor for bass on the push.
body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and figure there's nothing to talk about. I've been running the same twenty-foot Lund out to the Isles of Shoals for going on eleven years and I can tell you thirteen miles is plenty if you fish it right. Most guys never leave the beach. I'm three miles offshore before the coffee's cold, anchored up on a piece of structure most of Hampton doesn't know exists, and I'm back at the ramp with fish in the box before the parking lot fills up. You don't need 130 miles of coast. You need to know your fifty yards.

This week that fifty yards was the north side of Appledore, out past the research station in that stretch of broken bottom where the ledge drops from 45 down to 70 feet. Haddock have been sitting tight to that structure on the slack tide, right at the top and bottom of the swing when the current lays down enough to hold bottom without a pound of lead dragging you sideways. Clam bellies on a standard two-hook rig, size 4/0 hooks, six-ounce bank sinker, and we've been picking through shorts to get to keeper haddock in the 20-22 inch class, mixed with a few cod in the 6 to 10 pound range that came up off the same piece. Nothing to write home about in terms of numbers — this isn't June, and the water's warmed enough that the bite window is short, maybe 45 minutes either side of dead slack — but if you're there when it turns, you're not going home empty.

What's telling is where the fish aren't. The open water between the mainland and the Shoals has gone quiet for groundfish, which tracks with what you'd expect this time of year — that water's pushing into the high 50s, low 60s at the surface, and cod and haddock want the cooler, structure-hugging water tight to the ledges where there's still some thermal relief and current to hold bait. I've stopped bothering with the mid-channel humps I fished in May. All the productive marks right now are hard structure, deeper water, close to the islands.

Mackerel showed up thick around the Shoals moorings and off Star Island in the last ten days, which is exactly the signal you want if you're chasing bass or targeting bigger groundfish, because mackerel strips and whole mackerel on a jig head are about as good a bait as exists out here in July. Snag a few on a Diamond jig or Sabiki rig before you set up on the bottom bite — costs you fifteen minutes and pays for itself.

Inshore, the story's been the stripers, and Hampton Harbor has been the most consistent piece of water in my zone all week. The pattern's simple and it hasn't changed in years: bass push into the harbor mouth on the last two hours of the incoming tide, working the deeper channel edges along the north jetty and up toward the Route 1A bridge, chasing pods of bunker and sand eels that get pushed up with the tide. I've had good luck throwing 3-inch white Slug-Go's weightless right along the rocks on the jetty, and when the current's really moving, switching to a half-ounce bucktail with a white curly tail trailer to get down into the seam where the bass are sitting on the structure waiting for bait to get swept past. Fish have run mostly schoolies and low-slot, 22 to 28 inches, with the occasional better fish mixed in on the harder tide stages. Seabrook side of the harbor's produced too, particularly right where the marsh creeks dump into the main channel on the last of the ebb — that's flounder water as much as bass water, and we've picked a few keeper flounder there on squid strips fished on the bottom with light spinning gear, though that bite's thinned out compared to June.

Bluefish have been scattered but present — a few boats working the rips off Great Boars Head have run into blitzes of medium blues, 3 to 6 pounds, chopping up bait on top mid-morning. Nothing sustained, more of a here-today, gone-tomorrow situation, but if you see birds working and bait skying, it's worth a few casts with a metal lip swimmer or a Hopkins jig before you move on.

Rye Harbor's outer breakwater has held some stripers on the dropping tide in the last hour of daylight — that's been a evening pattern more than a morning one, fish sliding out with the current and feeding along the rocks where the baitfish get funneled through the gap.

Looking at the week ahead: the tides are building toward the new moon, which means bigger swings and stronger current — good news for the Hampton bite because more water movement means more bait getting pushed through that harbor mouth and more reason for bass to stack up on the structure. If the wind stays out of the southwest and lays down like it has been, I'd be back out at the Shoals working that same stretch off Appledore on the slack, and I'd have a mackerel jig rigged before I even set the anchor. The groundfish bite is thin but real if you're precise about tide stage. The bass bite in the harbor is the more dependable of the two right now — less finesse required, more about being there on the right two hours of tide.
